summary: Describes the RELATIONAL extension to the Sieve mail filtering language, adding relational operators such as greater than or less than to its tests. It can compare content and also count entities in header and envelope fields. It was replaced by RFC 5231.

plainLanguage.summary: Mail filters can already check whether words match. This adds is it more than, or less than, so a filter can for instance react to how many addresses are on a message. It was replaced by RFC 5231.

questions: how to count recipients in sieve
sieve value and count match types
subtitle: Add comparison operators to the Sieve mail filtering language.

tldr.problem: Sieve mail filters can check if text matches a pattern, but cannot compare values numerically or count how many items appear in a message field.
tldr.mechanism: The RELATIONAL extension adds two match types: VALUE for comparing strings relationally, and COUNT for counting entities in fields and comparing the count to a number.
tldr.outcome: Mail filters can now sort by priority level, count recipients, or compare addresses alphabetically. This extension was later obsoleted by RFC 5231.

today: RFC 3431 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2002. It was obsoleted by RFC 5231, which is the current definition of the Sieve relational extension.

sections.title: Introduction to the Extension
sections.content:
Sieve is a language for filtering e-mail messages at delivery time. It runs on mail servers and is designed to be simple and safe—it has no variables, loops, or ability to shell out to programs, making it suitable for environments where users cannot run arbitrary code.

The RELATIONAL extension adds relational operators to the existing address, envelope, and header tests in Sieve. This lets scripts compare field values (like checking if a priority is greater than 3) and count the number of entities in a field (like checking if there are more than 5 addresses in the to and cc fields combined).
sections.plainLanguage: Sieve is the mail system's set of rules for sorting mail. This extension lets those rules ask 'is this bigger' or 'is this smaller' instead of just 'is this exactly equal'.

sections.title: The VALUE and COUNT Match Types
sections.content:
The extension defines two new match types that extend the capabilities of Sieve tests.

VALUE match type performs relational comparisons between strings. It takes values from the message (after removing leading and trailing whitespace) as the left side and compares them to values in the test expression as the right side using operators like gt (greater than), ge (greater than or equal), lt (less than), le (less than or equal), eq (equal), and ne (not equal). If multiple values exist on either side, the test succeeds if any pair satisfies the comparison.

COUNT match type first counts the specified entities in the message, then compares that count to the values in the test expression using the same relational operators. The Address test counts recipients in specified fields; the Envelope test counts recipients in envelope parts; the Header test counts the total number of field instances. When multiple field names are specified, counts are added together.
sections.plainLanguage: VALUE lets you compare text, like 'is this sender's name after M in the alphabet?' COUNT lets you count things, like 'are there 3 or more addresses?'.

sections.title: Practical Examples
sections.content:
A filter can use VALUE to check an x-priority field: header :value "lt" :comparator "i;ascii-numeric" ["x-priority"] ["3"] moves messages with priority less than 3 to a Priority folder.

Another example uses COUNT to flag messages with many recipients: address :count "gt" :comparator "i;ascii-numeric" ["to"] ["5"] marks messages with more than 5 people in the to field as likely SPAM.

Addresses can be sorted alphabetically: address :value "gt" :all :comparator "i;ascii-casemap" ["from"] ["M"] puts mail from senders whose name starts with N–Z into one folder and A–M into another.

The extension also supports combining conditions. For instance, checking both that only one person is in to and cc combined, and that person is the script owner, puts the message into an "Only me" folder.
sections.plainLanguage: You can now write rules like 'if there are more than 5 people getting this mail, it is probably spam' or 'if the sender's name starts with a letter after M, put it in this folder'.

sections.title: Security and Implementation
sections.content:
The extension requires support for the i;ascii-numeric comparator, which MUST support at least 32-bit unsigned integers (larger integers MAY be supported). This comparator does not support negative numbers.

A critical security requirement is that implementations MUST ensure the envelope "to" test reflects delivery only to the current user, preventing users from determining whether a message was delivered to someone else. Similarly, the envelope "from" field counts zero when MAIL FROM is blank, or one when not blank, preventing privacy breaches.
sections.plainLanguage: The system must be careful with the envelope 'to' field—it should only show you what is delivered to you, not reveal mail sent to others. And numbers should work with regular, positive integers.

sections.title: Status and Relationship to Other RFCs
sections.content: RFC 3431 extends RFC 3028, which defines the Sieve mail filtering language. The Sieve extension uses the RELATIONAL capability keyword to declare support. The extension also references the i;ascii-numeric comparator defined in RFC 2244 (ACAP) and conforms to RFC 2119 keywords and RFC 2234 ABNF notation.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an add-on to the main Sieve system (RFC 3028). It follows the same rules and uses a standard way of comparing numbers from another protocol.
